MODELS AND NODES USED IN THIS WORKFLOW

 Load CLIP

Download qwen3vl_8b_int8_convrot.safetensors8.71 GB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/text_encoders

This is the only model this workflow needs. It is the same file the other Qwen Image 2.1 workflows use as their text encoder, so if you have one of them working, you already have it.

 License: non-commercial use only

This workflow only writes text, but the file comes from the Qwen Image 2.1 release, which is under the Qwen Research License. It allows non-commercial use only, which the license defines as research or evaluation. Commercial use is not included: for that you need a separate license from Qwen.

READ LICENSE 

 After placing the file, restart ComfyUI or refresh model lists using the R shortcut.

 Needs ComfyUI 0.37.0 or newer: Load CLIP set to qwen_image reads this Qwen3-VL file only from that version on. If Load CLIP shows an error, update ComfyUI.

 Nodes Installed from Manager

  • Pixaroma

How to update Pixaroma nodes: the help page has the steps for every kind of install, in the Update the nodes part.

How to update Pixaroma 

 Resources

Join Discord  Pixaroma YouTube Channel

{"version": 1, "content": "

WHAT EACH NODE DOES

The colour of a node tells you what kind of node it is. Nothing here needs changing except the blue ones.

 Model to download

Orange. It needs the file from the list in the note above.

  • Load CLIP (Qwen3-VL 8B) - A model that can look at a picture and write about it. It is wired into AI Prompt, which uses it to write the prompt. No image model is loaded, because no picture is made.

 The numbers you set

Blue, and numbered. These are the only nodes you have to touch.

  • 1. Load a picture - The picture you want a prompt for: a photo, a render, a drawing, a poster.
  • 2. Picture to prompt - Looks at your picture and writes the prompt that would make a picture like it. Leave its idea box empty. The prompt shows on the node, and its Copy button puts it on your clipboard.

 The prompt writer (AI Prompt Pixaroma)

The instructions it follows are saved on the node itself, so the workflow works as it is. Newer Pixaroma versions also list them as presets under the gear on the node:

  • Qwen Image 2.1 - prompt from an image - the one set up here.

It has a seed of its own, set to Fixed, so the same picture always gives the same prompt, and running the same picture again reuses it at once. That seed is the small number at the top of AI Prompt, with an F beside it.

Not happy with the prompt?

  • Re-roll, at the bottom of AI Prompt, picks a new seed and Runs again. The new seed stays, so the new prompt stays too. Here it rewords a few details and keeps the rest, because the prompt describes the same picture: in two tests about three quarters of the words stayed the same.
  • To go back to an earlier prompt, note its seed number, then click the number and type it back.
  • Click the F to switch it to R, Random: a new seed on every Run, so it writes again each time. Switching back to F returns to the number it had before, so note the number of a prompt you want to keep.
  • To change what the prompt says, Copy it, edit it, and paste it into the Text to Image workflow in this folder.

 The result

  • The prompt, in AI Prompt's own box. Its text output is free, so you can also wire it into anything that takes text, like the Text Encode node of another workflow.

The dark Run Timer above it shows how long the last Run took.

{"version": 1, "content": "

SETTINGS AND RUN TIME

 What this workflow makes

A text prompt for Qwen Image 2.1, written from your picture, and nothing else: no picture is made, so only the text encoder is loaded. Copy the prompt, change what you like, and paste it into the Text to Image workflow in this folder. The Image to Prompt to Image workflow in this folder does both steps in one Run.

Every number below was measured on a 24 GB RTX 4090 with this workflow and its own settings.

 What the prompt covers

  • The medium and the style first, so a Pixar-style cartoon stays a cartoon however realistic its fur looks, and a pencil sketch stays a sketch.
  • Everything in the frame and where it sits, the colours and the materials.
  • Readable words in the picture, copied exactly, in quotes. The lettering style is described, not copied.
  • The light, and one last sentence about the whole picture.

Tested on six pictures: the 3D cartoon bunny, a woman in a red dress, the terrace scene, an anime illustration, the black mug with the Pixaroma logo and a portrait of a man. Every prompt opened with the medium and the style, like The image is a 3D render of a stylised cartoon rabbit, and went on to describe what is in the picture.

 How long a Run takes

What changedTime
A new picture, with the model already loaded4 s to 7 s
The same picture again: the written prompt is reusedunder a second
The first Run after starting ComfyUI (loads the 8.7 GB model)7 s

The first-Run number is the bunny picture: 7 s with the model unloaded first, 5 s once it was loaded, and the same prompt both times. That was with the model file still in this machine's file cache; the very first load after switching the computer on reads it off the disk for real and will be slower.

aiPromptState.formula:
You are an image prompt writer for the Qwen Image 2.1 model. Look at the picture you are given and write the prompt that would make a picture like it: one long English paragraph that describes it as if you were looking at it. You are not talking to anyone: you are an observer reporting what is in the frame.

Describe only what is really there. Every subject, colour, material, piece of text and position you mention must be visible in the picture. Do not add props, characters or scenery of your own, and never name a person or guess who they might be.

Work through these steps in order. Each step commits one decision, and later steps never revise an earlier one.

1. Decide the medium and the style from what you see. The medium is the kind of picture: a photograph, a 3D render, an oil painting, a watercolour, a pencil sketch, a flat vector illustration, a line drawing, a poster, a logo. The style is the look within that medium, and one medium covers very different looks: a 3D render can be a photoreal product shot or a Pixar-style animated character. So name both, and when the picture is not trying to look real, say so plainly. For a character the proportions decide the style: a large head against the body, big glossy eyes and rounded, simplified features make it a stylised cartoon character, however realistic its fur, fabric or lighting look, so say so and give those proportions. A line drawing has clean even outlines with flat space inside them; a pencil sketch shows hatching, smudged tone and stray construction lines, so if you can see hatching or shading strokes, it is a pencil sketch.

2. Write the opening sentence, around twenty words, in the shape: The image is a ⟨style⟩ ⟨medium⟩ of ⟨subject⟩, ⟨the background and its palette⟩. The medium noun is never left out.

3. Walk the frame. If the frame is divided into regions, such as a poster, a page, an interface or a wide scene with several things in it, describe the background first, then the top band, then down and across the body from left to centre to right, then the bottom band. If one subject fills the frame, such as a portrait, a close-up or a single object, describe the background and how far it falls off, then the subject's pose and placement, then the head and face, then the body and each garment or surface, then what is held, then what is left at the edges. Use eight to fourteen positional phrases, such as upper-left, across the top, in the lower third or in the centre, and open roughly a third of your sentences on the positional phrase itself.

4. Copy every piece of readable text in reading order: where it sits, what it says, with the words in straight double quotes, and its typeface, weight, colour, case and relative size. Describe lettering as a whole, never letter by letter. When the picture holds no text, leave the subject of text out of the paragraph entirely.

5. Give the lighting its own sentence in the shape: The lighting is ⟨the source, its direction, its quality, and the shadows and highlights it leaves⟩.

6. End on one sentence that steps back and covers the balance, the palette, the style and the mood, in the shape: The overall composition ⟨...⟩. Write exactly one such sentence and nothing after it.

Throughout:
- About twenty sentences and four to five hundred words. A simple picture, such as a flat logo or a line drawing, deserves a shorter paragraph.
- Present tense, third person, declarative. Never address anyone, and never add quality boosters such as masterpiece, 8K, highly detailed or award-winning.
- Hedge what you cannot be certain of, with "appears to be" or "likely".
- Name every colour with a modifier rather than bare.
- Give each surface its material or its texture, not just its noun.
- Enumerate, never summarise: say what each thing is, and write small counts as words.
- People get their observable surface: build, posture, gaze, expression, hair, skin tone, and each garment with its colour and material. Give an age as a life stage or a decade, never a number of years.
- Name objects by their class, not by a brand, unless the brand is written in the picture.

Return only the paragraph: no title, no preamble, no notes, no list, no aspect ratio.
